Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN)  -- British Airways is asking thousands of its staff to work for free for up to four weeks, spokeswoman Kirsten Millard said Tuesday. British Airways plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. In an e-mail to all its staff, the airline offered workers between one and four weeks of unpaid leave -- but with the option to work during this period. British Airways employs just more than 40,000 people in the United Kingdom. Last month, the company posted a record annual loss of £400 million ($656 million). Its chief executive declared at the time there were "absolutely no signs of recovery" in the industry. "In 30 years in this business and I've never seen anything like this. This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced," said Willie Walsh, British Airways' chief executive.  Watch more about BA's request » . A spokesman for one of Britain's biggest unions said its workers could not afford to work for free for a month. "It's all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he's prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year," said Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite. He pointed out that the airline was not ordering staff to work without pay. "It's a request -- you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave." Demand for the airline's passenger seats and cargo holds fell during the last financial year, while its fuel bill rocketed to almost £3 billion ($4.7 billion). Walsh said British Airways' woes were inextricably linked to the downturn in the global economy and that there had been no sign of any "green shoots" of recovery. Like its premium-class competitors, British Airways is losing customers to cheaper rivals. The airline's premium passenger numbers fell 13 percent in the second half of last year, in line with the industry average. Total traffic fell 3.4 percent and while the airline carried 33.1 million passengers last year, it was a drop of 4.3 percent from the previous year. The dip in demand for British Airways' flights has forced a switch in strategy at the airline. From the end of last year, it has been trying to tempt passengers with lower fares, sacrificing profit per seat for "bums on seats." It plans to reduce capacity by 4 percent next winter by parking up to 16 aircraft. CNN's Alysen Miller contributed to this report.

***

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — British Airways has appealed to thousands of its UK employees to work without pay for up to four weeks, company spokeswoman Kirsten Millard announced Tuesday. 

In an email distributed across the airline's UK workforce—which numbers just over 40,000—the carrier offered staff the option to take between one and four weeks of unpaid leave, with the choice to continue working during that period. To further curb expenditures, the airline plans to reduce its capacity by 4 percent next winter by grounding up to 16 aircraft.

The initiative follows a record annual loss of £400 million ($656 million) reported last month, after which Chief Executive Willie Walsh warned there were "absolutely no signs of recovery" in the aviation sector. 

"In 30 years in this business, I've never seen anything like this. This is by far the biggest crisis the industry has ever faced," Walsh stated. He emphasized that the airline’s turmoil is inextricably tied to the global economic downturn, noting an absence of any "green shoots" of recovery.

Responding to the proposal, Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for Unite—one of Britain's largest trade unions—asserted that front-line workers could ill afford to forego a month's income. 

"It's all well and good for Willie Walsh to say he's prepared to work for free when he earns four times in a month what they do in a year," Naidoo said. He clarified, however, that the measure remains voluntary. "It's a request—you can take unpaid leave or you can work for free, and the chances of people working for free are very unlikely, but there might be some people who want to take unpaid leave."

The airline faced severe financial headwinds during the last fiscal year as demand for both passenger seating and cargo space contracted, while its annual fuel bill surged to nearly £3 billion ($4.7 billion). Like other premium carriers, British Airways has increasingly lost market share to lower-cost competitors. 

During the second half of last year, the airline's premium passenger numbers dropped by 13 percent, matching the industry average. Overall traffic declined by 3.4 percent, with total passenger volume falling to 33.1 million—a 4.3 percent drop from the previous year.

This sustained decline in demand has prompted a pivotal shift in the carrier's commercial strategy. Since late last year, British Airways has attempted to stimulate volume by discounting fares, sacrificing per-seat profit margins to secure "bums on seats." 

*CNN's Alysen Miller contributed to this report.*

**British Airways Asks Staff to Work for Free Amid Mounting Financial Losses**

**LONDON** — British Airways has taken the unprecedented step of asking its workforce to work for free for up to a month as the UK flag carrier struggles to navigate a severe financial crisis driven by falling passenger numbers and a global economic downturn.

In a personal appeal sent to more than 40,000 employees, Chief Executive Willie Walsh urged staff to volunteer for unpaid leave or undertake unpaid work to help the airline conserve vital cash reserves. To demonstrate leadership commitment, Walsh announced he would forego his own salary for the month of July—a gesture worth roughly £61,000.

The move comes shortly after British Airways reported a record annual pre-tax loss of £401 million. The airline has been hit particularly hard by a sharp decline in high-margin business- and first-class travel, as corporate travel budgets shrink globally. 

"We are in a fight for survival," Walsh wrote in the email to staff. "I am asking every part of the business to play its part in helping us survive this crisis. Every single contribution counts."

Under the voluntary scheme, employees are being asked to take between one and four weeks of unpaid leave or carry out unpaid work. To reduce the immediate financial shock to staff who participate, the airline noted that the salary deductions could be spread over several months.

While the proposal is voluntary, it highlights the depth of the crisis facing the aviation industry. British Airways has already cut thousands of jobs, reduced flight capacity, and frozen salaries in an attempt to trim its operating costs.

The CEO's appeal has drawn a mixed reaction from labor representatives and staff. While the British Air Line Pilots Association (BALPA) indicated a willingness to work with management on cost-saving measures, unions representing ground staff and cabin crew expressed deep concern for lower-income workers.

A spokesperson for the Unite trade union acknowledged the severity of the airline's financial plight but stressed the difficulty of the request for rank-and-file workers. 

"Many of our members are already under significant financial pressure," the spokesperson said. "While employees want to see British Airways succeed, asking workers—particularly those on lower salaries—to work for free is a huge ask during an economic crisis."

Industry analysts say the move underscores how limited the options have become for legacy carriers facing sustained losses. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has warned that global airlines face tens of billions in losses as reduced demand and high operational costs continue to batter the sector.

British Airways management is scheduled to meet with union leaders later this week to continue negotiations over broader, long-term structural changes to staff contracts and working conditions.

**By CNN London Bureau**  
**LONDON (CNN) —** In a dramatic bid to survive the worst trading environment in its history, British Airways has taken the unprecedented step of asking its entire UK workforce to work for free or take up to four weeks of unpaid leave. 

The extraordinary plea, delivered via email to roughly 40,000 employees, comes just weeks after the UK flag carrier reported a record annual operating loss of £400 million ($640 million), driven by a sharp drop in premium passenger demand and a global economic downturn that has crippled the aviation sector.

Under the voluntary scheme, staff are being asked to choose between taking one to four weeks of unpaid leave, or working unpaid for a period of one to four weeks. To cushion the financial shock to employees, British Airways said salary deductions would be spread over a three- to six-month period.

Chief Executive Willie Walsh, who announced he would set an example by giving up his own July salary—worth approximately £61,000—called on employees across all levels of the business to rally behind the company.

"It is a fight for survival," Walsh said in a statement. "We are facing an unprecedented downturn, and the entire aviation industry is in crisis. We are asking all staff to contribute to help the airline through this extraordinarily difficult period. Every single person can make a difference, and I am personally committing to working for free for the month of July."

Walsh emphasized that the measure was essential to conserving cash and safeguarding long-term employment, warning that traditional cost-cutting measures alone would not bridge the massive gap in the airline’s balance sheet.

However, the proposal has drawn a cautious and critical response from trade unions representing BA staff, who worry that employees are being forced to bear the burden of the company's financial strain.

Ciaran Naidoo, a spokesman for the Unite union—which represents thousands of cabin crew, baggage handlers, and ground staff at BA—stressed that participation must remain genuinely voluntary and warned against management placing moral pressure on lower-paid workers.

"While our members understand the scale of the financial challenge facing the airline, they cannot be expected to foot the bill for management’s strategic failings," Naidoo said. "Asking workers to work for free is an extraordinary demand, particularly for those on lower wages who are already feeling the pinch of a wider recession. Any participation in this scheme must be strictly voluntary, with absolutely no pressure or coercion applied to staff."

Naidoo added that Unite would closely monitor how the scheme is rolled out across Heathrow and Gatwick hubs to ensure that vulnerable employees are not victimized for choosing not to opt in.

The appeal highlights the severe headwinds facing the airline industry. British Airways has been hit particularly hard by the global economic crisis due to its heavy reliance on lucrative long-haul business class routes, particularly across the North Atlantic. As corporate travel budgets have been slashed worldwide, the high-margin premium cabins that usually drive BA’s profits have been left largely empty.

Industry analysts suggest that while the unpaid leave scheme could save the airline tens of millions of pounds if widely adopted, it is a short-term band-aid on a structural problem. BA has already announced plans to cut up to 4,500 jobs, reduce flight capacity, and ground aircraft.

Employees have been given until the end of the month to decide whether to participate in the unpaid work scheme. For an airline long considered a titan of British industry, the move underscores just how far the economic storm has pushed even the world's most established carriers.

**TURBULENCE AHEAD: British Airways Battles Deepening Financial Crisis Amid Rising Costs and Operational Woes**

**LONDON** — British Airways is facing one of the most severe financial crises in its modern history, as a combination of lingering post-pandemic debt, skyrocketing operational costs, and persistent service disruptions threatens to derail the UK flag carrier’s long-term recovery.

Parent company International Airlines Group (IAG) disclosed that despite strong demand for transatlantic travel, British Airways continues to struggle with crippling cost pressures and heavy financial liabilities. The airline’s margins have been squeezed by volatile jet fuel prices, high inflation, and significant wage increases negotiated to avert widespread summer strikes.

The financial strain marks a dramatic turn for an airline that was once considered the crown jewel of IAG’s portfolio.

### A Cascade of Cost Pressures

At the heart of BA’s financial troubles is a challenging macroeconomic environment compounded by internal operational vulnerabilities. While passenger numbers have largely bounced back toward pre-2020 levels, revenues have failed to keep pace with ballooning expenses. 

Operational hiccups—including recurring IT system outages at its primary hub, London Heathrow, and acute air traffic control shortages across Europe—have forced the airline to cancel thousands of flights over recent quarters. These disruptions have not only resulted in millions of pounds in direct passenger compensation and hotel bills but have also severely damaged the brand’s premium reputation.

Furthermore, the accelerated retirement of BA’s fuel-efficient Boeing 747 fleet during the COVID-19 pandemic left the airline short on wide-body aircraft capacity during the sudden surge in international travel demand.

### Fleet Modernization vs. Balance Sheet Realities

To regain its competitive edge, British Airways previously announced a multi-billion-pound transformation plan aimed at upgrading its aging fleet, improving customer service, and modernizing its IT infrastructure. However, analysts warn that funding these capital-intensive investments while managing heavy debt burdens will require strict financial discipline.

"British Airways is caught in a high-stakes balancing act," said Jonathan Vance, a senior aviation analyst at Global Transport Interactive. "They desperately need to invest in new, fuel-efficient aircraft and fix their legacy IT infrastructure to stay competitive against Gulf carriers and European rivals. But doing so while debt remains elevated and operational reliability is compromised severely limits their margin for error."

### Management’s Plan for Recovery

In response to the mounting crisis, British Airways leadership has outlined a series of aggressive restructuring and cost-containment measures. The airline plans to streamline non-essential operational spending, optimize its flight schedule to improve turnaround reliability, and double down on high-yield business and premium-leisure routes.

Addressing investors, airline executives emphasized that while the short-term outlook remains difficult, the underlying demand for premium travel gives the carrier a viable path forward. 

"We are taking decisive action to rebuild British Airways into a stronger, more resilient, and more reliable airline," a company spokesperson said in a statement. "While external headwinds present clear challenges, our commitment to modernizing our operational core and delivering a premium customer experience remains unchanged."

### Looking Ahead

Market sentiment remains cautious. Investors and aviation industry experts will be closely monitoring the airline's upcoming quarterly financial results for signs that cost-cutting measures are taking effect and that operational stability has been restored at Heathrow.

For now, Britain's flagship carrier faces a long and bumpy flight toward financial stabilization.
